set.tovw: Grade B (court/probate thread): placed on the 1877/78 Sauk County map
set.st: Garrison was a deserted village site near the lower narrows of the Baraboo River, named for Andrew Garrison, who built a mill and settled there about 1848. Mrs. Ann Garrison made the place famous by "salting" a mine, building a pottery and keeping a ferry across the river, and she was postmaster in 1858. The 1877/78 Sauk County map prints GARRISON beside a platted block on the west bank where the Baraboo turns north through the Lower Narrows, with a saw mill (dam site) just ENE; gone from the c.1915 plat. Pin is on the 1877/78 village block, not a find spot. LiDAR cache check (USGS 1 m, 2020): Nothing that fits the story stands out within the search area: the pits and lines it finds there are ditches, banks, ponds or natural ground.
set.pl: West bank of the Baraboo River at the Lower Narrows: platted block on the 1877/78 Sauk County map, saw mill (dam site) just ENE
pinev: Village-level: the 1877/78 Sauk County map prints GARRISON beside a platted block on the west bank where the Baraboo turns north through the Lower Narrows (about 400 m); the old pin was about 1 km NE.
set.t: About 3 hours from Eau Claire. The 1877/78 map puts the village block on the west bank at the Lower Narrows with the saw mill just ENE: look there for the mill dam, ferry landing and pottery. Potsherds and kiln waste would mark the pottery. Permission: check ownership; river bank.

set.tovw: Grade B (court/probate thread): placed on the c.1915 plat
set.st: In January 1937 the Wisconsin Rapids Daily Tribune called Progress, in the town of Rock, a "ghost town", in the obituary of Mrs. Christina Anderson, one of Wood County's oldest pioneers, who was "identified from its beginnings" with it. The c.1915 plat shows Progress as a platted railroad village in the SW¼ sec 33 T24N R2E at the south edge of the town of Rock; called a ghost town by 1937. Pin is on the platted village, not a find spot. LiDAR cache check (USGS 1 m, 2022): Nothing that fits the story stands out within the search area: the pits and lines it finds there are ditches, banks, ponds or natural ground. The 1912 Rand McNally index lists Progress, Wood County, map square L-18, as a railroad station. (The index places it only to the map square, so it confirms the name and the railroad, not the exact spot.)
set.pl: Platted railroad village, SW¼ sec 33 T24N R2E, south edge of the town of Rock, Wood County (c.1915 plat)
pinev: Village-level: the c.1915 plat shows Progress as a platted railroad village in the SW¼ sec 33 T24N R2E (about 400 m).
set.t: The c.1915 plat places the village in SW¼ sec 33 T24N R2E by the railroad: check the 1938 aerial for the old lots and depot site. Only about 1 h 45 min from Eau Claire. Permission: private land.

pinev: 1902 Hovey & Frame Atlas of Warren County p.17 (T77N R23W) shows the 123-acre Dixon strip on the E edge of sec 23 with the house just W of the 23/24 line (130th Ave); matches the 1909 news (2 mi NW of Palmyra, ~10 mi NE of Indianola) and the 1930s aerial farmstead. Pin confidence B (plat-placed).
